During this escalatory phase, we expect a strong upward impact on oil and gas prices as geopolitical risks increase. With flows through the Strait of Hormuz drying up over the weekend, freight rates are likely to rise as well. It also implies our scenario with the largest energy price increase has become more likely; we see the potential for spikes to triple-digit levels in this case. Of the scenarios we test, this has the highest price upside, but we would expect most of the impact to be mitigated given the large US naval presence. Three additional offsets to supply increases are 1) OPEC+ supply increases (though a Hormuz closure would impact these volumes as well); 2) pipelines in Saudi Arabia and UAE can divert significant (~5mbd) volumes; 3) high oil stocks in China reduce the need for China to backfill the Iranian cargoes it might lose; and 4) significantly floating oil cargoes as Iran increased its production ahead of the strikes. These circuit breakers imply we see a relatively limited structural increase in energy prices after likely initial spikes. In a regime change scenario we could see a potentially lengthy and challenging power vacuum. In this scenario, we would expect to create a strong price peak that eventually recedes to structural upsides of USD10/bbl for Brent and EUR5/MWh for TTF

On the whole, while spending cuts featured largely in recurrent items, the authorities have raised allocations to capital and financial assets by some ZAR8bn, or 0.1pp of GDP — a step in the right direction, given the potential positive effect on growth. Liquidity Coverage Ratio Regulators could also tweak the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) to lower aggregate bank reserve demand. The standard LCR requires that banks with total assets exceeding $700bn hold enough high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to cover net cash outflows in a stress event. Banks larger than $250bn in assets but below $700bn are bound by either the full LCR requirement or a less restrictive version depending on their reliance on short- term wholesale funding (STWF). Smaller banks have no LCR requirements unless they have high dependence on STWF, which we showed in the regression above to be meaningful for reserve demand. We extend the prior chart’s scope to include the GSIB banks subject to the full LCR requirement and find that their weighted average reserves as a % of liabilities is about 3 percentage points higher than that of Category IV banks. records.text: al 15y current coupon has looked particularly wide to 30y current coupon mortgages ( Exhibit 35 ). Historically, 30-year current coupon OAS has traded wider than 15-year current coupon OAS, with one of the reasons simply being that 15-year mortgages, by definition, have shorter duration and therefore simply cannot extend as much as their 30-year counterparts, providing investors with a better convexity profile. In turn, investors typically require more OAS to compensate them for taking on the greater negative convexity risk associated with 30-year mortgages vs. 15-year mortgages. Compression in Treasury OAS between 30-year and 15-year current coupon conventionals began around March 2025, after the 15y/30y basis reached the tights (Exhibit 36 ). Since then, the spread between the two terms has been a one-way street, and 15y current coupon first printed wider than 30y current coupon in November 2025, with the difference widening ever since (Exhibit 36 ). 15-year conventional current coupon OAS recently touched almost 15bp wider than 30-year, when prior to a few months ago, 15-year spreads had almost always been tighter.

Past rounds of fighting have shown that the economy can absorb short-lived disruption with limited casualties and damages in Israel relatively well. The drawdown to annual GDP is here mostly confined to services consumption that cannot be stockpiled or fully made-up for after the security threat subsides, e.g. dining, entertainment or education. A longer security threat logically extends this lost economic activity, but an equally important mechanism here is the loss of labour input due to large-scale reservist call-ups, as was the case in the first months after October 7th 2023. That said, the end of this round of conflict could again result in an upside outcome for the Israeli economy in the form of a reduced risk premium. This, however, requires a successful operation that palpably and lastingly lowers the security threat the Iranian regime poses. records.Author: Alexandre Stott
records.text: Services inflation in the Euro area has been stickier than expected, with the n year-over-year rate standing at 3.2% in January—nearly unchanged from last May. This remains above the 2-3% range historically consistent with 2% core inflation, given historical core goods inflation of 0-1%. The three most plausible explanations for this are (1) a robust labour market, (2) services prices still catching up to relatively higher goods prices, and (3) wage growth running hotter than usual. These mechanisms are challenging to disentangle, as they operate n simultaneously and interact with one another. However, the Euro area offers the unique advantage of cross-country comparisons, enabling better identification of each driver. We therefore use a quarterly panel of the 10 largest economies since 2000 to regress services inflation on these three drivers and other control variables. Our results suggest that all factors—labour market tightness, the relative price of n services to goods, and wage growth—have contributed to boosting services inflation in recent years. The recent moderation was largely attributable to diminishing catch-up effects as the services-to-goods price ratio normalised. In contrast, a weak labour market and relatively lower goods prices acted as headwinds during the 2010s. Our model suggests that services inflation remains more elevated than normal due to remaining services price catchup (worth 0.4pp), resilient labour markets (0.5pp) and firm wage growth (0.3pp). O

We assess that these developments are unlikely to be a game-changer for the euro area macroeconomic outlook. Prior to the ruling, and reflecting the trade policy framework established under the summer 2025 EU–US trade deal, European exports were already facing an average tariff rate of around 12%. This comprised a 15% tariff on car exports, a 50% tariff on steel and aluminium products and a reciprocal 15% IEEPA duty applied to non-exempt sectors for which the US most-favoured-nation rate fell below the 15% threshold. Under the post-ruling setting, and with broadly no change to sector-specific (Section 232) duties or exempted sectors, the introduction of a 10% surcharge is likely to result in a net decline in the effective tariff rate applied to European exports – albeit by a margin too small to have any meaningful impact on euro area growth under standard trade elasticities: in a study released on 21 February, Global Trade Alert estimated that, following the latest developments, the weighted average tariff rate (using 2024 US import values as weights) would stand at around 10.5%. records.text: The Risks to Energy Prices From Iran Q0. What has happened in the Middle East over the weekend? Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has been killed after Israel and the US launched an ongoing military operation against Iran’s leadership and military. Iran has responded by firing ballistic missiles and drones at US assets and allies across the region, targeting Israel, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Jordan. Q1. What is the evidence on disruptions to energy flows? Have you changed your baseline energy price forecasts? While flow data through the Strait of Hormuz through last Friday point to somewhat above annual average volumes for oil (Exhibit 1) and for LNG (Exhibit 2), there have been reports over the weekend of large drops in the number of tankers crossing through the Strait, and of three oil tankers reportedly damaged in the region. We think traffic may remain disrupted until there is further clarity on risks (e.g. mines, strikes). We assume no sustained flow disruptions in our baseline energy price forecasts, which we have left unchanged for now, and we will continue to monitor high frequency flows through the Strait closely. records.text: 27 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 34 Deutsche Bank AG Narrowing the full set of banks down to those with assets between $50bn and $250bn for a closer comparison, we regress reserves as a % of total liabilities on a dummy variable for banks with assets greater than $100bn and add the following control variables: wholesale funding as a % of total liabilities, deposit funding as a % of total liabilities, and long-term securities as a % of total assets (since higher unrealized losses may have increased some banks’ desire to hold reserves). We find that banks subject to ILST testing have 2.7 percentage points higher reserves as a % of total liabilities after accounting for the control variables, statistically significant at a 95% confidence level. The other significant variable in the regression is wholesale funding, which makes sense as that is a determining factor in whether a bank is subject to the LCR requirement (to be discussed in the next section). Using the 2.7% of liabilities difference in reserves as a rough approximation for the restrictiveness of ILSTs, we estimate that ILST requirements are boosting aggregate reserve demand by roughly $400bn. This aligns with Bowman’s instructions to supervisors last fall to allow banks to count potential FHLB liquidity in their ILSTs. records.text: Overall, Fed speakers continued to suggest that the FOMC will keep rates unchanged at the next couple of meetings. St. Louis Fed President Musalem (non-voter) argued that policy was neutral and that risks to employment and inflation are roughly balanced. Chicago Fed President Goolsbee stated that he would want to see evidence of inflation heading back toward the 2% target before lowering rates again. Nonetheless, he expressed confidence that rates would be lowered "several more times this year" if disinflationary progress materializes. Boston Fed President Collins also argued that further cuts will be conditioned on disinflationary evidence and that it will likely be appropriate to remain on hold for some time, with the policy stance "mildly restrictive, perhaps quite close to neutral already. " Notably, even the most dovish voters appear to be moderating their views. Governor Waller, who had dissented in favor of an additional rate cut in January, stated that he could support a pause in March, especially if the labor market data showed continued improvement in February. Governor Miran, who has dissented in favor of additional easing in all but one meeting since joining the Board in September 2026, advocated for four 25bp cuts this year, and sooner rather than later. Even so, this is incrementally less dovish, as his dots from the December SEPs had indicated 150bp of cuts in 2026. records.text: US Supreme Court is poised to rule on the legality of tariffs implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Commentary around the case appears to suggest a ruling against the tariffs is the most likely result, but the US administration has already indicated that tools and measures are ready for quick deployment to fill the gap. We think this outcome probably creates a new tariff regime, moving away from broad-based measures to become more region- and sector-focused. One possibility is fresh or more aggressive Section 232 tariffs, which have already caused considerable pain for Canada’s economy with 50% duties on steel and aluminium. The breadth and quantity of goods that are vulnerable to new levies make Canada quite vulnerable to this outcome. Macroeconomic fundamentals and monetary policy: The Bank of Canada appears unwilling to ease further, and has left the policy rate steady at 2.25% for the last two meetings. Officials see current policy at about the “right level” and believe monetary policy can play only a limited role in helping the economy through this structural shock. We detect some openness in the language about the direction of the next move, and markets are pricing in about 6bp of cuts through mid year, but 5bp of hikes by year-end accordingly. 27 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 18 Deutsche Bank AG Appendix A: Definition and methodology Twin deficits and twin deficits score: Twin deficits are one of our preferred measures of fiscal policy space. In addition to the conventional twin deficit calculation, which is simply the sum of the projected Budget & Current Account deficit of each country data from the IMF's World Economic Outlook (WEO) database, we have also created a "twin deficits score”. For each year, the twin deficits score is a weighted average of the previous years' twin deficits. We assign a higher weight to this year’s Twin Deficit (t), followed by gradually lowering the weights of the past five years (t-1, t-2, …, t-5) twin deficits and finally adding some weight to the cumulative twin deficit up to year t-5. This allows us to create a synthetic twin deficit score which combines both the most recent flows and the historical stock of budget & current account deficits. Considering the fundamental difference between Norway and other G10 countries, we make adjustments to Norway's twin surpluses and NIIP when mapping with its market pricing. Net international investment positions (NIIP): NIIP is a measure of a country's reliance on foreign funding and, empirically, it is highly correlated with 10-year and 30-year government bond yields in cross-sectional regressions. records.text: We anticipate that the Mexican peso will remain extremely sensitive to any developments or news related to the USMCA as the July 1st review date approaches. Should the US threaten to fully withdraw from the agreement, the MXN could experience a sharp depreciation similar to the substantial decline witnessed in early 2017. Banxico would also likely respond by raising interest rates to stabilize the currency and anchor inflation expectations. Since “Liberation Day” (April 2), MXN has appreciated steadily, moving from around 20.0 to 17.20 today. The rally has been supported by a weaker USD backdrop, Banxico’s cautious stance, and strong inflows into EM carry trades. Implied volatility has declined as spot strengthened (Figure 7). With vol still low and options priced cheaply, we see value in adding option protection ahead of July 1. To sum up, with USMCA negotiations underway , and tensions potentially rising , it seems prudent to buy protection through options. We anticipate that the risk premium could climb as the July review date draws closer. records.text: atory missile strikes against US bases and regional allies. In addition to Israel, missiles were fired toward Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Bah- rain, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, and Qatar. We cannot confidently map the military or political path ahead, but recognize that this event generates greater macro- economic risk than recent military conflicts — the US inter- vention in Venezuela or the Israel-Iran conflict. Through its potential to disrupt global energy markets and supply-chains, it connects more closely to the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. It is also similar to the Russian invasion in that it looks likely to have material, lasting political and economic consequences at the regional level. The main uncertainty is whether this conflict proves disrup- tive and/or turns into a lasting conflict like the Russia- Ukraine war. The central 2026 Global Macroeconomic Out- look issue relates to the global supply of crude oil and natural gas. The regional concentration of global oil and gas supply flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and heightened uncer- tainties around the nature of the conflict point to elevated tail risks. Channeled through our models, a sustained reduction of roughly one-fifth of this supply — in the range of 4mbd per day — would be sufficient to push Brent crude well above $100bbl. The credit market remains in a strategic mid-cycle regime which implies tight spreads and low volatility over time. But not all the time. At the start of 2026 spreads are tighter, consensus expectations are bullish on both growth and Central Banks, and positioning is longer. None of this is extreme but warrants a tactically neutral beta view, in our opinion. Credit Outlook – February 2026: Slow Down! Expectations are now higher: Unlike six months ago, today the consensus is bullish on growth and expects dovish Central Banks, although Kevin Warsh’s would-be appointment should probably remove some of the more extreme dovish policy outcomes. Longer positioning has brought us closer to neutral. Nothing here is extreme yet, but the hurdle for positive surprises is higher (Figure 1). Supply no longer scarce, but not yet abundant: For the past two years corporate bond scarcity has suppressed both spreads and spread volatility but even so there have been periodic buying opportunities. Now that corporate bonds are no longer scarce there’s even more reason to anticipate spread spikes. New risk reduction views – reducing beta from long: Reducing beta, even if more tactically, is mainly about having positions that are not primarily relying on spreads going tighter. records.text: 27 February 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Week in review ECB money and credit data In January, corporate loan flows declined, driven by a continued weakening in Germany, and also a large decline in France (more than offsetting the strong rise in December). The weakening in Germany stands in somewhat of a contrast with the recent PMI and Ifo survey data. Household lending softened a little compared to December, but was still strong. A decline in German lending growth was offset by recoveries in Spain and France. The credit impulse (the change in net lending), which is a leading indicator of private domestic demand, weakened further this month, driven by the decline in corporate lending growth, and by Germany. The overall level of the credit impulse suggests domestic demand is likely to track sideways, at levels close to trend. The Bank Lending Survey, itself a leading indicator of the credit impulse, suggests slowing credit conditions are unlikely to see a resurgence in the credit impulse in the very near term. The picture coming from the bank lending channel data suggests that while the transmission of previous monetary policy has helped contribute to the domestic resilience we have seen in 2025 and through to today, the strength of this support continues to fade as we move further away from the previous rate cutting cycle. records.text: Natural Gas Q10. How much risk premium has been embedded in European gas prices? Differently from oil, we believe that until this past Friday, European natural gas prices had embedded little-to-no risk premium associated with Iran-related geopolitical risks. Specifically, TTF has been pricing in the bottom half of our estimated hard-coal-to-gas (C2G) switching range for the past month, modestly below our 36 EUR/MWh March 2026 TTF forecast (Exhibit 11). Once accounting for the recent sell off in carbon emission prices to below the 80 EUR/t embedded in our TTF price forecast, worth 2.0-2.5 EUR/MWh in gas-equivalent terms, prompt gas prices are still largely in line with our view that TTF needs to be in this C2G switching range to help manage NW European gas storage to above 80% full by end-Oct26, given that current inventory levels remain well below average. That remains our view, and we maintain our 34 EUR/MWh balance-of-the-year TTF price forecast. Q11. What are the risks to global gas prices from this weekend’s developments in the Middle East? We see significant upside risk to European gas and global LNG prices. The most significant impact to global gas markets would come from a potential disruption of the approximately 80 mtpa (302 mcm/d or 11 Bcf/d, 19% of global LNG supply) of LNG that typically flow through the Strait of Hormuz (Exhibit 2), which could potentially arise from an escalation of the ongoing conflict. Despite escalating geopolitical risks, the oil market entered the current crisis in a position of significant oversupply. Over the first two months of the year, we estimate the global balance was running at roughly 1.4 mbd surplus, providing an initial buffer against short-term disruptions. Still, sizable volumes of crude remain stranded in export‑constrained countries like Russia and Kazakhstan, keeping global crude exports about 1 mbd below 4Q25 levels (Oil Demand Tracker: Strong demand, bottlenecked inventories, US gasoline prices tick up, 27 February 2026). If the war extends beyond 25 days, producers will be forced to physically shut-in production across the Gulf. This could temporarily remove up to 16 mbd of crude and product exports transiting the Strait of Hormuz—a volume far exceeding immediately deployable spare capacity elsewhere in the system, as nearly all effective global spare capacity is itself located within the Persian Gulf. Oman, which was initially spared on February 28, was targeted the following day when drones struck the commercial port of Duqm (Arab News, March 1, 2026). In our view, the immediate spillover effects extend well beyond the missile strikes themselves. The IRGC declared the Strait of Hormuz “effectively closed, ” with several oil companies and firms pausing shipments (Bloomberg, March 1, 2026). Airspace was shut down across eight countries, grounding Dubai International Airport—the world’s busiest international hub—and temporarily halting operations at Emirates, Etihad, Qatar Airways, and dozens of international carriers (The National, February 28, 2026). We believe that for a region that has spent decades positioning itself as a stable and cosmopolitan hub insulated from the Middle East’s longstanding instabilities, 28 February prompts a meaningful reassessment of regional risk. records.text: Market Pricing Q4. What risk premium is the oil market pricing? We estimate the risk premium embedded in crude prices stood at $7/bbl on Friday evening as the difference between the Brent Friday close of $72 and our $65 estimate of fair value based on fundamentals such as OECD stocks. Based on the 15% gain in the WTI retail trading product, we estimate a real-time risk premium embedded in crude prices of $18/bbl. This corresponds to the 98th percentile since 2005. Call options offering upside protection embody a larger premium with 3 month 25-delta call skew at the 100th percentile of the distribution of the last 15 years already as of Friday. Q5. How does that real-time risk premium translate in oil supply disruptions? The $18/bbl real-time risk premium estimate corresponds to the market pricing a 1-year disruption of 2.3mb/d to global supply or approximately a 1-month full halt in Strait of Hormuz flows (though allowing for spare pipeline capacity use as a partial offset).4 Scenarios Q6. records.text: In equities, the impact of a risk and growth shock is clearly negative, but only a severe and sustained oil price disruption (as in 1990 or 2022, for instance) would have large effects on the global growth picture. Geographically, oil-importers are clearly more exposed (including markets like Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Turkiye and India) and within the major markets the US is generally relatively better placed than many others. Cyclical sectors are likely to see pressure in this scenario, particularly consumer-facing areas, including airlines, and industrial oil users. Energy producers should outperform. Some of these cyclical sectors and markets have had a strong start to the year and might be more vulnerable to position adjustments. The impact on credit markets is likely to be similar—a net widening of spreads but with a strong distributional tilt, favoring energy producers at the expense of consumers and cyclicals. Within the EM credit universe, even some of the GCC oil exporters are likely to see a widening in spreads similar to October 2023 with weaker sovereigns more reliant on capital inflows among the most vulnerable. We would expect equity volatility to rise and continue to think that long volatility expressions like these, which are highly negatively correlated with equities/credit and quite liquid, are good portfolio additions. records.text: On party strategy: French local elections use a two- round system, and the distribution of seats makes sure the winning party gets a comfortable majority to rule. However, there is a low bar to qualify for the second round – a candidate only needs to secure above 10% of the vote. This opens the door to a second round that includes more than two parties and thus increases the chances of a surprise result. On the right of the political spectrum, having lost ground at the national level over recent years, the right-wing conservative party, Les Républicains (LR) and other centre-right parties will likely use this election to demonstrate they are a credible alternative to RN. This raises a question over any second rounds where a left-wing candidate leads after the first, and both LR and RN cross the threshold for inclusion. Will one drop out to favour the other? Or will they both stay in and split the right-wing vote? Such decisions could reveal the degree of political animosity/flexibility between the two parties as the presidential election approaches. It is a similar story on the left where the Socialist Party has officially split from LFI, opening up the same potential dilemma. We will watch for signs LR can still get support from rural municipalities and regain big cities like Paris or Lyon from left-wing parties. As we laid out earlier this week, the process to challenge and then replace a Labour leader is an involved one and we still think it more likely that any challenge would come after the local elections in May. Given the success of the Greens, who ran on a firmly left-of-centre agenda, this week's result is also likely to increase pressure on the prime minister to move his policy agenda in that direction. However, the fiscal rules — which we continue to expect will be met — would continue to constrain how much he is able to do through extra borrowing. As a result of US sanctions on Iran, Japan has halted crude oil imports from Iran since May 2019. However, Iran accounts for around 4% of global crude oil production, meaning any impact on Iranian output would likely push crude oil prices higher. The situation would become more serious if Iran, in response to a US attack, were to strike US military bases across the Middle East, leading to a broader regional conflict, or if Iran were to block the Strait of Hormuz. Around 95% of Japan’s crude oil imports come from Middle Eastern countries (2024), and roughly 80% of tankers bound for Japan pass through the strait. As such, a closure of the strait could cause Japan’s crude oil imports to plunge temporarily. That said, Japan maintains a certain level of petroleum stockpiles (as of end-December 2025, 146 days for state reserves, 101 days for private reserves, and 7 days for joint stockpiles with oil-producing countries, for a total of 254 days), meaning that domestic oil supplies would not be cut off unless the closure were prolonged. In addition, China’s presence is expected to act as a deterrent against a strait closure, given that China accounts for around 90% of Iran’s crude oil exports (2024, WSJ). records.text: 226/02/2026 High participation rate: Except for the Covid-disrupted 2022 vote, local elections in France usually have the highest turnout after the presidential vote. Turnout has averaged between 65–70%, suggesting to us that the results can be a good gauge of French political sentiment ahead of the next national elections. Caution is still needed, however, because there remains a significant bias towards local issues when voters cast their ballot – which tends to favour incumbents and therefore adds a degree of latent stability. National interest: However, we think this might be a bit different next month for two reasons. ▪ The 2022 local elections suffered from a markedly low turnout because of the pandemic, so we think the results may not have fully reflected the electorate’s true preferences. That creates a higher risk of sharp swings this time around. ▪ National issues appear to be influencing voter intentions more strongly. It is even more the case for urban vs. rural municipalities. In 2020, 58% of voters said their choice was driven primarily by local concerns; that share has fallen to 53% overall and to 48% in larger cities (see Figure 2). Surveys reflect that in a rising share of respondents who say they will be equally weighting local and national considerations. Security has become an ever more potent concern – and resonates at the local level as well as nationally. A new head of the IRPG has been announced (Majid Khademi), while Khamenei’s successor is yet to be chosen (Aljazeera, 01-Mar-26). Iran’s constitution explicitly anticipates sudden leadership loss. As explained in a Foreign Policy magazine article (Iran Is Built to Withstand the Assassination of Ayatollah Khamanei): “Article 111 stipulates that if the supreme leader dies or becomes incapacitated, authority transfers immediately to an interim council composed of the president, the head of the judiciary, and a senior cleric selected through the Expediency Council. The goal is to keep leadership steady, not to change the political system. Importantly, the constitution lists the qualifications for the next leader but does not limit the choice to a strict religious path. This flexibility allows succession to be a process of negotiation and stability, not just a religious decision. There is no set deadline for picking a new leader. If there is a war, the interim council can lead for a long time. What might look like delay from the outside is actually a way to manage risks inside the country. ” So, even though (according to some specialists) Iranian long range missiles may not last longer than a fortnight, one cannot totally disregard the possibility of a slightly protracted conflict and subsequent impact on global asset prices. Markets sold off in response. 'Ghost GDP' defies basic income identities Such an Armageddon scenario has a number of inconsistencies. Most fundamentally, it conflicts with macroeconomic income and expenditure identities. There can be no 'ghost GDP' (defined in the report as 'output that shows up in the national accounts but never circulates through the real economy'). If soaring unemployment and a resulting drop in labour income brings a collapse in consumption (C), but GDP (Y) remains high regardless—ie, as 'ghost GDP'— something else must rise: either investment (I), net exports (NX) or government spending (G). That's the expenditure identity: Y = C+ I+ G+ NX. And since NXs even out globally, the accounting for the global economy is simply Y = C + I + G. Ghostbusters! On the income side, Y translates into wages (W), profits (P) and net taxes (NT). Y = W + P + NT . Hence, if under a given Y, the labour income (wages) collapses, capital income (profits) rises, assuming unchanged NT . It also holds that the income side must equal the expenditure side: every dollar earned must be either spent or saved. In Mexico, annual inflation at the start of 2026 has increased with headline at 3.9%, from 3.7% at the end of 2025, and core at 4.5% y/y, from 4.3% y/y last year. Nonetheless, we highlight that this acceleration has been smoother than we had expected. The inflation print for the first half of February indicated that ongoing effects from excise hikes – most notably those targeting beverages and tobacco – are already easing. Furthermore, after a thorough examination of the items that could be affected by the tariffs imposed on imports from non-FTA countries since the beginning of the year, we have found little evidence of transfer to consumer prices. Meanwhile regarding core dynamics, we highlight that the housing component seems to be returning to its pre-pandemic dynamic. Moreover, if not only the surplus but also foreign-currency- denominated assets were drawn down and converted into JPY to fund the measure, the JPY conversion would effectively amount to FX intervention, meaning approval from the US Treasury might be required, while at the same time raising questions over the appropriateness of reducing foreign exchange reserves that are, by nature, intervention funds, for other purposes. No, while our simple static model directly relates net exports from the Middle East to global and OECD inventories, the actual fair-value effects likely rise disproportionately with the length of the disruption. If the disruption lasted ¼ of a month, the hit to production would likely be very small as producers would likely continue to store oil on land, and delay rather than significantly cut cumulative exports. Moreover, producers such as Saudi Arabia have precautiously increased exports and production ahead of the escalation. In contrast, if oil were to be trapped for four months in the region and because inventories can’t draw persistently, oil prices would likely rise disproportionately to balance the market via price-driven demand destruction and refinery run cuts. At current output rates, that equates to about 22 days of stranded crude production (Figure 5). Additional buffer may come from shipping availability. Based on our analysis below, we conclude that 25–7y JXs are cheap and 35–6y JUs are rich. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 426/02/2026 Preview for September senate election: For any future president, the support of the Senate could be crucial. In terms of fiscal policy, the National Assembly has the final word, but the upper chamber still debates, and can amend, government proposals. Unlike the Assembly, the Senate cannot bring down a government, yet it also cannot be dissolved; therefore it functions as a stable counterweight to the executive. Moreover, the constitution cannot be amended without the Senate’s consent, giving the chamber a legitimacy comparable to that of the Assembly. For the far-right parties, and for LR leader Retailleau, who advocate lower spending on immigration policy to reduce the budget deficit, a change in the constitution will likely be needed. At-risk seats: Historically, voters tend to stick with incumbents in Senate elections, which has given traditional parties an advantage; RN currently holds only three Senate seats, while LFI has none. For the Senate, half of the seats are renewed every three years. The last half renewal took place in 2023. At present the Senate is controlled by right-wing parties: the conservative LR has 130 seats and the centre-right holds 59, giving the right-leaning bloc a total of 189 seats (174 seats for a majority). In an environment of risk down and oil prices up, the Dollar should still be the haven of choice, second only to the Japanese Yen, while fundamental beneficiaries like NOK tend to only outperform other risky currencies on a relative basis. While the Dollar’s observed correlations have shifted somewhat in the last year, it is different when the shocks are global. There are a number of fundamental and technical reasons why the Dollar tends to benefit from global shocks that impair both risk sentiment and the real economy. Many oil exporters are also exposed to global growth, and therefore the risk beta tends to dominate if sentiment deteriorates sharply. If the commodity effects are durable even after the initial market disruption—which would have some parallels to 2022—the distributional effects can start to reassert themselves in FX, as they have in recent weeks. records.text: 1 For a comprehensive analysis of how new technologies/products diffuse and the phenomenon of 'growth' from microorganisms to societies and cities, see Vaclav Smil: Growth - from microorganism to megacities (2019) Theorising the GDP ghost of 'singularity' Can there be higher investment without hiring someone to do the work and paying them wages, which translates into consumption? Let's do a thought experiment to test the extreme scenario: a world without private consumption or government expenditure (C = G = 0), implying that all the economy's output is investment (Y = I). On the income side, no wages are paid and there are no net taxes (W = NT = 0) and all economic income accrues to capital as profits (Y = P). Hence, Y = I = P = S. To put this into words, all production is investment activity, which fully translates into capital income, which in turn is entirely saved and invested again (ie, all demand is investment demand). This would require that the machines, structures, software, robots, etc constituting investment are machine made: ie, machines extracting the resources, robots building robots, and AI models training AI models. Capital goods are used to produce more capital goods. In this world, firms would sell to firms, which receive all the profits and fully reinvestment them. Hence, the final output would be capital formation, which then leads to more capital formation. In this C= 0 world, humans would be irrelevant (no longer exist?). Y = I = P = S. Welcome singular

records.text: In equities, the impact of a risk and growth shock is clearly negative, but only a severe and sustained oil price disruption (as in 1990 or 2022, for instance) would have large effects on the global growth picture. Geographically, oil-importers are clearly more exposed (including markets like Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Turkiye and India) and within the major markets the US is generally relatively better placed than many others. Cyclical sectors are likely to see pressure in this scenario, particularly consumer-facing areas, including airlines, and industrial oil users. Energy producers should outperform. Some of these cyclical sectors and markets have had a strong start to the year and might be more vulnerable to position adjustments. The impact on credit markets is likely to be similar—a net widening of spreads but with a strong distributional tilt, favoring energy producers at the expense of consumers and cyclicals. Within the EM credit universe, even some of the GCC oil exporters are likely to see a widening in spreads similar to October 2023 with weaker sovereigns more reliant on capital inflows among the most vulnerable. We would expect equity volatility to rise and continue to think that long volatility expressions like these, which are highly negatively correlated with equities/credit and quite liquid, are good portfolio additions. What this change would do is allow banks to buy bonds into HTM and hedge interest rate exposure without having to apply any spread changes to earnings or concern about LCR impact, perhaps resulting in banks needing less reserves as well. Thus, for instance, a bank could buy a 30yr treasury, asset swap it, and have ~70bp of spread income booked for the life the Treasury without having to worry about the spread volatility on its earnings too much. Or for our investors, banks could buy something fixed rate that is easy to hedge - say agency CMBS, deep discount mortgages, well structured CMOs, call protected pools, etc, asset swap them, and make say 75bp on DUS or 80bp on discount MBS. In other words, this very much aligned with our thematic view that less regulation will bring back to the mortgage market, and also that mortgages are more likely to outperform swaps than Treasuries as this likely causes more buying of UST vs swaps from banks as well.

Rate cuts: The market has moved closer to our view that the BoE will deliver a 25bp rate cut in March (c.80% priced in at the time of writing). This follows February’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting which showed a closer-than-expected vote on whether to hold or cut (5–4 to hold). Meanwhile, the accompanying forecasts and rhetoric from Governor Andrew Bailey aligned with our view that UK inflation can continue to fall this year. We see headline inflation making downward progress towards the BoE’s 2% target, particularly from April. We think this expectation will be enough to prompt another 25bp rate cut in March. From then, we think the BoE will be able to cut further, down to a 3% terminal rate (deeper than the market currently prices in). Our 10Y Breakeven model utilizes the following explanatory variables: n University of Michigan 5-10y inflation expectations, which allows us to estimate long-term inflation expectations. n Input prices, 6m ahead, Dallas Fed services survey, which gives information on expected domestic inflationary pressures and wage pressures. n Prices paid for raw materials, 6m ahead, KC Fed manufacturing survey, which accounts for expectations of supply-side inflationary pressures. n Monthly change in gasoline prices, which accounts for the energy component of CPI. Our EUR 10s30s Term Premium model utilizes the following explanatory variables: n EUR 5s10s Term Premium, which serves as a baseline for term premium across the curve. n EUR 1y30y NVOL, which reflects the convexity benefit of flattening 10s30s; higher volatility should therefore decrease 10s30s term premium. records.text: 2 GEMs Viewpoint | 01 March 2026 Asia: Impact due to energy exposure Claudio Piron Merrill Lynch (Singapore) claudio.piron@bofa.com Chun Him Cheung, CFA Merrill Lynch (Hong Kong) chunhim.cheung@bofa.com The traditional and expected response for Asia FX should be short-term managed depreciation due to Asia’s net energy dependency. Specifically, THB, KRW, SGD, and INR should be sensitive to any sustained rise in oil prices as crude oil imports are estimated at roughly 6.8%, 4.6%, 4.5% and 3.8% of their respective GDPs. More specifically, sustained higher energy prices pushed Korea’s trade balance to deficit in 2022. Meanwhile, even if China’s crude oil dependency ranks lower (1.8% of GDP), about a third of China’s crude supply comes from ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz. This said, China dislikes excessive volatility and will focus on ensuring CNY depreciation will be orderly. This could be defined as a move in USD/CNY spot (currently around 6.8621) back towards the USD/CNY fixing of around 6.922 over the course of a week. Regional geopolitical implications are also key Beyond the transmission of shocks through economic and financial channels, the implications for Asia’s own regional geopolitics will also be key. Compensation per employee—the broadest measure of pay pressures in the economy—stood at 4% year-over-year in 2025Q3, above the 2.5-3% range we estimate to be consistent with 2% inflation. Importantly, wages are a separate driver of services inflation because pay pressures do not only reflect labour market tightness. Workers also bargained for higher wages because elevated goods prices had raised their cost of living. This wage catch-up mechanism is distinct from the Phillips curve channel described above, but similarly led firms in the services sector to pass higher labour costs through to consumer prices. Disentangling these mechanisms empirically is challenging, as they operate simultaneously and interact with one another. However, the Euro area is unique among developed markets in offering the opportunity to study variation in services inflation and its drivers across countries. This approach also helps circumvent two limitations of Euro area data: its relatively short history and measurement inaccuracies. It is one of our favourite empirical strategies in the Euro area, and we have previously used similar frameworks to study the drivers of wage growth and the household saving rate. Since 1979, there have been eight notable instances of regime change in medium-to-large scale oil-producing nations, each with significant implications for global oil prices and supply dynamics (Figure 6) . While demand conditions and OPEC’s spare capacity significantly shape the overall market impact, these events typically lead to a substantial spike in oil prices, averaging a 76% increase from onset to peak. Initially, oil prices rose by about 5% in the first month, but over a three-month period from the onset of the conflict, they averaged a 30% increase, eventually stabilizing at levels around 30% higher than pre-conflict levels (Figure 7). This pattern aligns with supply disruption trends, where in the initial month, only about 2% of supply on average was lost, but significant supply losses occured over a six-month period, averaging around 23%. These supply losses are challenging to recover quickly, further supporting elevated prices. As seen in the arrow in Figure 10, we can basically describe convexity value as the change in value which is not explained by linear approximation or by dv01. Figure 11 shows such a difference in both absolute price and percentage price change (versus the nearest price). We can see the convexity value is of similar shape to a quadratic function, so we estimate such a value by a quadratic function of yield change, that is, 0.5*C*(yield change)^2, where C refers to convexity (0.5 is just a scalar for a mathematical reason). As Figures 10 and 11 show, the convexity value increases if the yield moves more. But yield can move a lot or a little, so we use expected yield change, which is 1 standard deviation, expressed in absolute yield changes, such as 20bp. Such yield changes (= volatility) depend on the holding horizon of the bond. records.text: ty is 2bp/day, then three months worth of volatility is 3*sqrt(64) = 24bp, assuming 64 business days for 3 months. Just like we assume a holding period for a carry/roll-down calculation, we do so for convexity so that we can think in terms of absolute volatility over the investment horizon. We get unit C (= convexity) by solving the below equation for C, as we set the yield change as 1bp as a unit value. (Actual price change for 1bp change – linear estimate)/price = 0.5*C*(unit yield change = 1bp)^2 In the above formula, we use percentage price change, just like duration. Therefore, convexity itself (as opposed to convexity value) is larger for low-price bonds (Figure 12). But actual value is reduced because price is low. Then, we convert the value into the yield equivalent by dividing by dv01. If the horizon volatility increases from 3bp/day to 4bp/day, then the convexity value increases by 1.7times (=16/9), which is an important element of convexity. We show the numerical example of Figure 12 in Figure 7 with JU14 and JU18. records.text: Q7. How much could the fair value of oil prices rise in key disruption scenarios? We think of Iran-related oil disruption scenarios as either reductions in Iran oil supply only, or disruption to broader regional oil shipping or production. Iran production disruptions: We estimate that a potential 1mb/d supply n disruption—which corresponds to half of Iran’s crude exports—for 12 months would boost the fair value of oil by $8 (although prices could rise more as escalation risks are reassessed). Broader production disruptions: Because Iran targeted oil producers across the n Middle East, we can’t rule out future damage to oil production/export infrastructure in the region. The most recent comparable event is Iran’s attack in September 2019 on the Saudi Abqaiq oil production facility, which caused the biggest ever single day oil production disruption and a nearly 20% intraday price move (although prices moderated as production fully recovered just over 10 days after the initial strike (Exhibit 9)). records.text: AI has probably been a net positive for employment so far. The left chart of Exhibit 7 shows that job categories exposed to the AI infrastructure build have added over 216k jobs relative to broader construction employment trends over the last few years, while the right chart shows that demand for AI-proficient workers has also increased by over 250k (=6½mn job openings * 4% of job openings referencing AI-related skills as a requirement). Combining these two estimates suggests that increased demand for AI-infrastructure builders and AI-proficient workers has probably more than offset any AI-efficiency related employment headwinds. Taken together, there is little evidence in the current data that significant job losses are imminent. What does historical evidence tell us about how AI will impact labor markets? Current data is inherently backward looking, however, and the current debate focuses on how AI will impact labor markets going forward. History provides some guidance on this front. Our baseline estimate is that 6-7% of workers (equivalent to 11mn jobs) will be displaced by AI automation. We arrive at this estimate by combining our assumption that full AI adoption will lift economy-wide labor productivity by 15% with our estimated historical impulse (Exhibit 8) that a 1pp increase in labor productivity driven by technological innovation leads to a temporary 0.3-0.4pp increase in the unemployment rate. Given that the Strait of Hormuz is the world’s most important oil transit chokepoint, disruptions in shipping could have profound consequences for the Gulf states, which account for around 22% of the world’s crude output. Our analysis suggests that Saudi Arabia and the UAE have the capacity to divert a meaningful portion of their current Arab Gulf exports through pipelines, which would partially alleviate the adverse effects major shipping disruptions. Oman maintains a strategic advantage in the face of significant maritime disruptions owing to its friendly long-term relations with Iran and its export outlets are situated to the East of the Strait of Hormuz. By contrast, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain, which do not have alternative export routes, would encounter a more challenging environment in the event of major shipping disruptions and/or a blockade of the Strait. Following adverse geopolitical developments in the region, evidence suggests that there has been a rerouting of oil trade flows away from the Bab el- Mandeb strait at the Red Sea’s southern entrance to the Cape of Good Hope, which increases the voyage by about ten days (Figures 10 and 11). Like Japan, China is heavily dependent on the Middle East for energy, and a closure of the strait would therefore deal a major blow to the Chinese economy. Taking into account its strong economic dependence on China, Iran may find it a difficult decision to block the strait. Even if it does not escalate to a closure of the strait, a prolonged period of military clashes around the strait or attacks on vessels would push crude oil prices higher and affect the Japanese economy. According to the EIA, the volume of oil passing through the strait has accounted for more than one quarter of global seaborne oil shipments in recent years, meaning the situation around the strait influences crude oil prices. In addition, around 70-80% of Asian LNG import prices are linked to the average CIF price of crude oil for Japan, so a rise in crude oil prices would also push up the price of LNG imported by Japan. Since mid-2022, crude oil prices have been on a declining trend, but if this were to reverse, it would generate upward pressure on import prices, JPY depreciation pressure via a deterioration in the current account, and, through these channels, upward pressure on consumer prices. According to a Cabinet Office macroeconomic model, a 20% rise in crude oil prices (in USD terms) would, in the first year, worsen real GDP growth by 0.12pp and the current account balance/GDP ratio by 0.44pp, while pushing prices up by 0.22%. records.text: Following the release of Claude Code and OpenAI Codex and recent commentary n on the potential of imminent job loss, market attention has shifted sharply toward AI labor disruption. In this report we frame our research on AI labor market disruption around the current debate and argue that near-term labor displacement concerns have become excessive. Because our baseline forecasts already incorporate our expectation that AI will n automate 25% of work tasks, recent events raise more uncertainty around timing than overall impact. We continue to expect a gradual adoption cycle—mostly because capability has not been the main barrier to technology adoption—but acknowledge that recent news raises risks of a more frontloaded impact. Concerns around an accelerated pace of disruption should be benchmarked n against the reality that AI’s labor market impact is still small. Sectors already affected by AI are creating a modest 5-10k drag on net job growth, but there is no broad correlation between AI adoption and labor market outcomes, and current use cases suggest only 2½% of US jobs are exposed to automation today. In fact, increased demand for AI-infrastructure builders and AI-proficient workers has probably generated a net positive hiring impulse so far. Historical elasticities suggest 6-7% of workers will be displaced under our n baseline forecast, which we expect will lower annual hiring by 1mn jobs and boost annual unemployment by a bit over ½pp under our baseline adoption scenario

We will be paying particularly close attention to three key dynamics. First, we will be watching the AI adoption rates in the Census Trends Business Outlook Survey (both for the overall economy and a broader set of industries than the narrow ones where AI is already having an impact) for any sign of inflection. A sharp turn in the next few months would suggest that the popularization of AI agents has put us on a new adoption trajectory. Currently this does not appear to be the case, as reported AI adoption ticked down by 1.4pp to 17.5% in today’s final February release. Current and past Fed officials agree that the forward guidance the FOMC implemented in 2020 alongside its adoption of the FAIT framework inappropriately prevented a timely response to the subsequent inflation shock (see A practitioner’s guide to forecasting in uncertain times ). The economic environment may have also contributed to the failure of FG during this period, as a rapid rebound with a sharp acceleration in prices was not well accounted for in the guidance. Warsh’s point is more that FG should not be used away from the ZLB. We find that services inflation accelerates after an increase in inflation expectations, labour market tightness, and wage growth, and after a decrease in the services-to-goods price ratio. Our results are also robust to alternative specifications that use the unemployment gap (relative to the European Commission’s estimate of the structural rate), the relative price of core goods (excluding energy and food), and unit labour cost (wage growth net of productivity gains). We can use our estimates to calculate the historical contribution of each driver to the deviation of area-wide services inflation from its sample average (Exhibit 4). This shows that a weak labour market, low inflation expectations, and the lower relative price of goods weighed on services inflation during the 2010s. However, the post-pandemic reopening and surge in energy prices reversed these dynamics in the early 2020s, with all factors—including wage growth—shifting to boost services inflation. Our estimates indicate that the recent moderation was largely attributable to diminishing catch-up effects with the normalisation of the services-to-goods price ratio. While recent company commentary and survey responses highlight risks of more significant displacement, the message is not universally negative. The share of companies mentioning AI when discussing hiring freezes or layoffs on earnings calls continues to trend up, and we found that these same companies have reduced job openings over the past year by a bit more than other firms. In addition, our survey of GS investment bankers last fall regarding client AI use suggests that large corporates expect significant headcount reductions due to AI in the near term to the tune of 4% over the next year and 11% over the next three years (left chart, Exhibit 10). Such headcount reductions would be much larger than historical evidence implies and highlight the potential for downside risks. At the same time, survey results published in a recent NBER working paper—which summarized responses from 6,000 CFOs, CEOs, and executives that are reweighted to match the economy-wide firm distribution in the US, UK, Australia, and Germany— suggest much smaller labor market impacts. As summarized in the right chart of Exhibit 10, the average US firm only expects a 1.2% headcount reduction over the next three years due to AI, with only 12% anticipating that headcount will be reduced by more than 5% (responses are similar for the UK but smaller in Australia and Germany). Along these lines, Dallas Fed President Logan suggested last year that the Fed could auction fixed quantities of discount window loans each day. Greater reliance on the discount window would allow for more reserves to be shed as banks would have a new source of same-day liquidity, but would also avoid risks associated with holding more longer-term or illiquid assets. Conclusion We will adjust our views as more information comes out, but for now these rough calculations suggest scope for reserve demand to decline by $400bn in the near- term through ILST easing and $300bn through LCR easing. Further out, this figure could be even higher if discount window borrowing is significantly expanded as a result of changes to the LCR. As shown in Exhibit 1, we estimate that AI will ultimately automate around 25% of all work tasks, particularly those that are routine and relate to information and data processing, content generation, and operations. While the recent news adds confidence to our long-standing view that AI automation will provide a significant macro shock, it does not suggest that the type of tasks that AI will automate has expanded. We are more sympathetic to arguments that the recent news suggests AI impacts could be more frontloaded than the 10-year adoption cycle embedded in our forecasts. But we see two reasons why a gradual and orderly adoption cycle remains the most likely outcome. First, spot data suggests AI adoption rates continue to only slowly rise despite significant model improvements over the last three years. The Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey reported that only 17.5% of US establishments are currently using AI for “any business functions” through February, with only 21.0% expecting to do so in the next six months. A very fast ramp-up in economy-wide production will likely be difficult. A widely-cited MIT report from August (which generated headlines that 95% of AI investments were yielding no productivity benefits) documented that top-down approaches to AI automation have largely failed, but use of AI models to automate specific pain points have been very successful. Another strong jobs print on top of January’s could strongly influence these discussions. Such a print could more conclusively put to bed arguments that the labor market is “flashing red” and that a rapid accumulation of labor slack is just around the corner. That could cause policymakers to see risks to monetary policy as more balanced and that rate hikes to counter excessive economic reacceleration are a sufficiently plausible tail risk in the near term to merit a change in language to signal a symmetric policy bias. In making such a language change, policymakers would likely intend to underscore their commitment to a steady reaction function through the leadership cutover, and implicitly to push back on widespread expectations for an abrupt dovish shift and a reduction in the data dependence of policy. Worth watching: Local elections in France typically have little immediate, major impact on government policy – but with a presidential race on the horizon, the 15 March and 22 March votes could deliver important signals on party strategy and prospects for 2027. In the past, when French politics was dominated by a right-wing bloc and a second group under the leadership of the Socialist Party, the signals sent by voting at local elections were sometimes seen as a useful barometer for the next general election, whether parliamentary or presidential. The Socialist local election success in 1977, for example, was interpreted as a foreshadowing of François Mitterrand’s win in the 1981 presidential election; conversely, a poor Socialist performance in the 1983 local elections preceded the loss in the 1986 parliamentary election. More recently, a strong local result in 2008 came to be read as an indication that François Hollande could win the presidency in 2012. Today the political landscape is far more fragmented, which may make it less straightforward to draw very emphatic conclusions from whatever transpires next month. records.text: G10 RATES | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY 27/02/2026 EUR rates: Curves steeper, spreads tighter Front end anchored: We project German 2y yields to reach 2.10% by end-2026, 10y yields to hit 3.10% and 30y yields to reach 3.85%. We still believe the European Central Bank’s next policy move will be a rate hike in Q3 2027, leaving the front end of the EUR yield curve largely range-bound for the rest of this year. Curves steeper: We continue to anticipate a steepening in EUR rates, reflecting the rise in term premia, as we forecast net supply, net of QT, in the eurozone to reach new highs this year (see 2026 EUR government bond and SSA issuance outlook, dated 12 January, and G4 supply update for 2026, dated 2 January). The Dutch pension fund transition should also continue to put upward pressure on the longer end of the curve. We note that around 65% of the industry is yet to transition, with around half of the January 2026 transition cohort to continue hedging gradually over the coming months. records.text: Ning Sun Noel Dixon 26 February 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General USMCA : What happens if US withdraws from agreement? The USMCA agreement is scheduled for its joint review on 1 July 2026. This review operates as a sunset clause, enabling the United States, Canada, and Mexico to address outstanding issues, update regulatory provisions, and strengthen supply chain resilience. Ideally, all participating nations will resolve substantive matters and agree to extend the USMCA through 2042. However, should consensus not be reached, the agreement will expire in 2036. The primary concern in these negotiations centres on the possibi lity of unilateral withdrawal, particularly if President Trump opts to exit the agreement, potentially resulting in its dissolution. Such an outcome would raise numerous questions: What role would the US Congress play? Would termination take effect immedia tely? What implications would this have for financial markets, and is this risk currently being priced in properly ? At the same time, some investors may have chosen to add the position and lowered the average book value, which seems to us the most likely reason why 35–36y richened. We saw another explanation for the richness, related to convexity. That is, as convexity is higher for low-coupon bonds (low price), it is natural that 35-36y is rich. records.text: Market Thoughts Following the Strikes in Iran The primary transmission channel of the Iran crisis on the global economy and markets is through its impact on energy markets. The initial market response is generally to raise risk premium on the back of higher uncertainty and wider distributions. Though not necessarily attributable to Iran and/or oil-related concerns, markets have recently incorporated some of the broader risks to the outlook, with growth pricing sitting firmly below our economists’ US baseline (Exhibit 1) and near-term inflation fixes moving higher into the weekend (Exhibit 2). But as it is typically hard to sustain broad-based pressure on economies or markets on the basis of uncertainty alone, it is likely that without sustained oil price shifts, the asset impact will begin to “localize,” shifting back towards directly affected assets. The impact of the energy price shock will depend on a combination of severity and expected longevity. Our commodity team has laid out the key risk scenarios, with the most damaging being a sustained full disruption to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Those disruptions have already begun, but a key question is how long they may plausibly last. In terms of the cross-asset impact, there are three important channels through which this kind of oil shock typically operates, beyond the initial increase in risk premium: A negative supply shock that increases the risks to growth on aggregate. 1. Our view for a while has been that the downside line in the sand for the unemployment rate – the level at which the FOMC would fear an acceleration in wages and in non-shelter services inflation – is around 4%. This is not certain and there are arguments that the labor market slack is lower, and declining more, than the unemployment rate suggests. For example, the prime-age employment-to-population ratio is at a long-term high, suggesting that, were we to see an unexpected cyclical pickup, the stock of available, experienced labor slack might prove limited. In addition to the policy bias shift discussed earlier, a strong report for February could coalesce the FOMC around a no-rate-cut baseline in 2026, down from the one-cut previously, via changes to the statement and the dot plot. We believe a n above 100k payroll print, a decline in the unemployment rate by at least a tenth, and stable or better participation rate could suffice.

While stopping the EUR 90bn loan to Ukraine would likely be good for spreads of EU bonds (as it would mean less supply, clearly in 2027), it seems likely that the European Commission (EC) and the EU Council will find a way to get the EUR 90bn loan done. records.text: For rates, the tension between inflation upside and growth downside of a negative supply shock will be key to the response. Our prior work on the sensitivity of inflation and real rates to oil prices shows that a 10% boost to oil prices tends to raise 2y breakevens by 15-20bp, with a smaller bullish impact on real rates, corresponding to a 5-10bp impact on 2y nominal rates. But we typically find that supply-driven oil price shocks have a significantly lower beta on traded inflation compared with demand shocks—a result consistent with the relatively muted reaction in US breakevens to the June 2025 jump in oil prices and the recent shifts in the inflation curve that, until late last week, appeared to reflect AI-related worries rather than energy price risks (Exhibit 4). This is likely because supply shocks often prove temporary, and also because of the negative risk reaction associated with supply tightening in energy markets, which drives down growth expectations and thus weighs on other sources of inflation. records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 01 March 2026 Citi Research 5 Trading geopolitics Historically, effects of geopolitical shocks have been short-lived. We typically see the impact of geopolitical crises through the lens of oil price moves. If oil prices spike, risk assets are usually negatively impacted. However, the shock wears off as soon as oil stabilizes. The average geopolitically driven oil price spike is very sharp, but not overly long lasting. For example, in the aftermath of Russia’s attack on Ukraine, which has been the largest recent shock, oil prices peaked a very large 34% higher, but it only took 7 days to get there. The SPX troughed the day oil prices peaked and rallied 17%, before falling again due to the Fed hiking cycle. As can be seen in Figure 6, this is the normal pattern even after large geopolitical shocks (after a month or so, often other macro factors take over, though, like COVID in 2020). For a more detailed discussion, see Geopolitics: Implications for the Economy & Markets. Smaller shocks, like the 2025 Iran attack, unwind even faster. As is illustrated in Figure 7, the two weeks before the 2025 strike, rates fell, equities were slightly lower, the USD was slightly stronger, Brent was up almost 20%, gold was up slightly, while base metals were lower. Two weeks later, equities were meaningfully higher, and the commodity moves had unwound to a large degree, while the USD weakened. Euro Area—Why Is Services Inflation So Sticky? Services inflation in the Euro area has been stickier than expected. The year-over-year rate stood at 3.2% in January, nearly unchanged from last May. This remains above the 2-3% range historically consistent with 2% core inflation, given core goods inflation of 0-1% (Exhibit 1). We see three plausible explanations for why services inflation has stayed high. First, the labour market remains robust. The unemployment rate stands close to estimates of the structural rate, and our broader measure of labour market tightness—which incorporates job openings and other indicators—suggests conditions are even firmer (Exhibit 2, left). Labour market tightness matters for services inflation because the services sector is highly labour-intensive. This is the core mechanism of the Phillips curve: when labour markets tighten, workers bargain for higher wages, and firms pass these costs through to prices. Second, services prices have been catching up to goods prices. The services-to-goods price ratio typically trends upwards—a pattern that is particularly stable when excluding volatile energy and food prices (Exhibit 2, right). Our prior work on the sensitivity of inflation and real rates to oil prices shows that a 10% boost to oil prices tends to raise 2y breakevens by 15-20bp, with a smaller bullish impact on real rates, corresponding to a 5-10bp impact on 2y nominal rates. But we typically find that supply-driven oil price shocks have a significantly lower beta on traded inflation compared with demand shocks—a result consistent with the relatively muted reaction in US breakevens to the June 2025 jump in oil prices and the recent shifts in the inflation curve that, until late last week, appeared to reflect AI-related worries rather than energy price risks (Exhibit 4). This is likely because supply shocks often prove temporary, and also because of the negative risk reaction associated with supply tightening in energy markets, which drives down growth expectations and thus weighs on other sources of inflation. records.text: Market Thoughts Following the Strikes in Iran The primary transmission channel of the Iran crisis on the global economy and markets is through its impact on energy markets. The initial market response is generally to raise risk premium on the back of higher uncertainty and wider distributions. Though not necessarily attributable to Iran and/or oil-related concerns, markets have recently incorporated some of the broader risks to the outlook, with growth pricing sitting firmly below our economists’ US baseline (Exhibit 1) and near-term inflation fixes moving higher into the weekend (Exhibit 2). But as it is typically hard to sustain broad-based pressure on economies or markets on the basis of uncertainty alone, it is likely that without sustained oil price shifts, the asset impact will begin to “localize,” shifting back towards directly affected assets. The impact of the energy price shock will depend on a combination of severity and expected longevity. Our commodity team has laid out the key risk scenarios, with the most damaging being a sustained full disruption to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Those disruptions have already begun, but a key question is how long they may plausibly last. In terms of the cross-asset impact, there are three important channels through which this kind of oil shock typically operates, beyond the initial increase in risk premium: A negative supply shock that increases the risks to growth on aggregate. 1. records.text: ws could change. The Fed’s Monetary Policy Report and associated Congressional testimony are mandated by law and we do not anticipate revisions to their structure or content. Conclusion Kevin Warsh’s nomination as Federal Reserve Chair could usher in a shift in central bank communication, potentially including a break from the post-GFC trend toward ever-increasing transparency. His nomination provides a timely opportunity to re- evaluate the Fed’s communication framework. Our views on how he will treat Fed communications include: Forward Guidance (FG) Under Scrutiny: Warsh has been an outspoken critic of using FG in "normal times." We expect him to lead a move away from its granular application, arguing its costs (impaired credibility, reduced flexibility) outweigh its benefits outside of a zero-lower-bound (ZLB) environment. The Dot Plot Will Be Downgraded, Not Destroyed: While Warsh may be skeptical of the dot plot, its complete elimination is unlikely to gain broad Committee support. Instead, we anticipate reforms designed to reduce its influence as a near-term forecasting tool. Possibilities include: shifting to rolling windows, focusing on a central tendency or range instead of individual dots, or embedding it within a broader discussion of risks and scenarios. Press Conferences to Continue, but with a New Tone: We believe Warsh will retain the every-meeting press conference schedule as a critical platform to frame the FOMC's narrative. However, the content will change.

records.text: Q&A on AI Labor Market Disruption Following the release of Claude Code and OpenAI Codex and recent commentary on the potential of imminent job loss, market attention has shifted sharply toward AI-driven labor market disruption. In this comment we frame our research on AI labor market disruption in the context of the current debate and argue that near-term labor displacement concerns have become excessive. Why have AI job destruction concerns shifted so sharply into focus? Concerns around AI labor market disruption have been present for several years now, but two catalysts have brought them sharply into focus in recent weeks. First, the release of new agentic models —namely Anthropic’s Claude Code and Open AI’s GPT-5.3-Codex—were widely viewed as a step forward in applied capability. While the evolution of models away from chatbots toward AI agents was under way for much of 2025, the ability of recent models to do a lot of work that humans currently perform on computers (while making fewer errors) has made the prospect of job task automation more real in the eyes of investors. Second, several high-profile essays from tech executives and researchers argued that AI models are increasing in capability at a pace that makes AI labor market impacts imminent. Most notably: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued in January that (among other things) the n speed, cognitive breadth, increased ability, and adaptability of AI makes it different than prior technologies while reiterating his pred

records.text: substitutes or complements white collar workers. As we showed in last year’s Barclays Equity Gilt study, Labour markets: AI transformation is still taking shape, available data provide little evidence that AI is displacing workers in occupations more exposed to disruption. If anything, we saw hints that the opposite was the case. Even if we take as given an off-baseline scenario in which (a) certain white-collar professions are entirely displaced by AI, and (b) that the market price of products and services that derive from these skills become cheaper, we think that historical experience provides helpful information about the aggregate economy's likely response. The time-honored reaction would be a compositional shift that moves productive resources toward products and services that derive from production processes that are not easily substituted with AI. This process has happened again and again, such as technological improvements in agriculture that helped displace demand to manufacturing goods over a century ago, and, more recently, improvements in manufacturing production that displaced demand to services. This process reflects human preferences: as with everything, our appetite for products that derive from fast cognition is subject to diminishing marginal utility. Idle minds ponder AI risks A quiet week for macro data left markets to ponder the darker side of AI: rapid disruptions, uncertain returns on massive capex outlays, and fears that productivity gains may arrive before incumbent businesses and the broader economy have sufficient time to adjust. This anxiety was amplified by a viral research note that sketched out a hypothetical risk scenario in which cascading disruptions push the unemployment rate to 10% by 2028, mostly reflecting the displacement of white-collar workers who perform tasks that may be displaced by AI (Bloomberg, February 24). records.text: Section 122 as placeholder: The administration appears to be employing Section 122 as an interim measure while it progresses towards more legally robust measures under Sections 232 (national security) and 301 (unfair trade practices). We ultimately think that a combination of Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs will be used to maintain broadly similar global effective tariff rates. At present, Section 232 tariffs apply to steel and aluminium, copper, lumber, automobiles and semiconductors (the latter two with specific exemptions). Nine additional investigations are underway, covering pharmaceuticals, critical minerals, aircraft, robotics and medical supplies. The administration has previously invoked Section 301 to raise tariffs on a range of Chinese products, although most of those tariffs originated during the first Trump term. A possible short-term scenario involves the use of Section 301 to re-introduce a fentanyl-related tariff on China. Further legal scrutiny likely: Section 122 requires a finding of “fundamental international payments problems”. The administration has indicated that a persistent current-account deficit intensfies this criterion; some commentators argue that, under a floating exchange-rate regime, a balance-of-payments problem may not exist. Discipline in reserve purchases (while it continues) lowers the probability that the next modification will be forced by markets. That could change if the country risk level does not fall below 400bp and trigger strong capital inflows. The persistence of country risk around 500bp could be signaling continued market doubts about both the level of the real exchange rate (because some capital controls remain in place) and the viability of this policy mix to simultaneously deliver higher net international reserves, solid economic growth and continued disinflation. If these doubts persist into H2 2026, we think the probability of a forced policy correction will rise quickly. In such a scenario, we would anticipate increased worries about external financing next year as well as concerns about the government’s ability to maintain high public approval levels (Figure 8) as the 2027 elections draw closer. For now, however, we believe the government is gradually regaining the benefit of the doubt through a healthy reserve accumulation policy.
