records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 01 March 2026 Citi Research 10 Israel macro assessment As one of the main participants, Israel stands to be noticeably impacted by the latest round of conflict; how much depends on the latter’s length and nature. Being obvious doesn’t make this observation any less important. Israel’s society and economy has in recent years shown that it can return to normality of daily life very quickly once security threats have subsided. It is more often the engagement beyond Israel’s borders – tourism, trade, capital flows, risk premia – that can take time to normalize. On the more optimistic side of the spectrum of possibilities, from an Israeli point of view, is a short-lived conflict, e.g. like the 12-day war last year, with limited damage in Israel, no on-the-ground engagement and a noticeably lower threat level from Iran going forward, be that due to regime change, instability within Iran or a palpably less aggressive approach from a successor regime in Iran. On the other end of the spectrum would be any outcome that requires Israel to commit significant numbers of military personnel, which would not only increase the risk of casualties, but also again weigh on the economy through constraining the labour force. Various outcomes in between would see something akin to the situation in place for much of the last 2.5 years; a functioning, but supply-constrained economy with a higher risk premium. We think labor market risk scenarios from AI are overstated Although we welcome discussion about downside risks, our views are fairly benign. Our baseline has always been that productivity gains from AI will be slow to materialize over the medium term, reflecting the rigidity of current production processes in the face of technological change. History is replete with examples in which large technological changes (such as advances in IT) diffused only gradually to measured productivity. Ongoing research suggests that this rigidity likely reflects structural features of the production process, rather than just resistance to technological change by workers or institutions. In particular, recent research by Chad Jones has shown that such rigidities can arise from the simple fact that the typical worker's production involves a combination of tasks, some of which are not easy to substituted with AI.4 These "weak links" , which include difficult-to-substitute tasks such as interpersonal communications (or even AI "hallucination" checks), substantially slow the diffusion of new technology. At this juncture, it is far from clear whether AI substitutes or complements white collar workers. records.text: CREDIT, COMMODITIES AND SUSTAINABILITY | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY Supply, infrastructure to dent US data center growth: Our latest study examined whether US energy supply can handle ever-increasing demand projections from the data centers at the heart of the AI story (see links opposite). In short, we see power supply and grid constraints as underappreciated risks, and our base case indicates a tight power system until at least 2030. Our base case is for 90GW of annual US peak power load growth from data centers alone by 2030 – about 16% of the potential load implied by utility resources planning estimates. Power market tightness would suggest either significantly higher peak power prices and lower system reliability, or a scaling back of uncommitted projects. We think the latter is more likely. Even if developers can absorb increased power generation costs, we would expect surging prices to pose a growing political challenge, particularly with US mid-term elections due in November. We see tightness easing by 2035, driven by incremental additions of renewables and nuclear, combined with a gradual normalization of gas turbine constraints and further grid reinforcements. Ultimately, project execution, policy support/stability, and the level of investment in grids and the energy transition will determine whether the outlook is dominated by either the ‘unconstrained-supply’ or ‘strong-headwinds’ supply scenario. As a reminder, we have written about FASB chances many times before, mostly leveraging the work of Todd Castagno, our head of Global Valuation, Accounting, and Tax. For instance, see the first change to allow prepayable assets in AFS to be hedged in 2017 using last-of-layer (Ready. Set. Hedge) and then the more recent change to allow banks to hedge using portfolio layer method hedging in 2021 (Can I Hedge It? Yes You Can). Oversimplifying, if a bank buys an asset into its available for sale portfolio, it can hedge with a portfolio of swaps (as long as the hedge is shown to be highly effective) and apply hedge accounting. That means that the asset and the hedge net out and the net is applied to earnings, with minimal impact to OCI and capital. Of course, there is spread risk in the bond as well, and spread changes do flow through to earnings and capital. Any losses in AFS would also result in less impact to liquidity as market value changes flow through to LCR. If a bond is bought into HTM, there is minimal impact to earnings or income statements, and simply PNL changes are disclosed in a fair value footnote, but right now they can't apply hedges to HTM securities. Of course, if there are too many unrealized losses, investors may raise concern (see SVB) so the duration of the HTM portfolio is still relevant. Warsh may object to this micro-managing of near-term market expectations, which can risk impairing credibility and injecting unnecessary volatility when conditions evolve in a way contrary to the guidance. The Dot Plot: Reform, Not Repeal Given Warsh’s distaste for forward guidance, a natural question is whether he will seek to reduce the influence of its primary vehicle, the dot plot within the SEP, or even eliminate it entirely. We believe the former is far more likely than the latter. Warsh has highlighted the pitfalls of being locked into a forecast: “Once policymakers reveal their economic forecast, they can become prisoners of their own words.” While this suggests he might support paring back the SEP, a full repeal of the SEP and its rate projections would mark a substantial about-face on transparency that would struggle to gain the support of the Committee as it is currently constituted. Instead, we see a path toward reforming the dot plot to reduce its influence. Plausible options include: 1. Convert to Rolling Windows: Shifting the SEP to rolling windows, rather than the current fixed calendar-based structure, would prevent the dot plot from giving explicit guidance on the timing of near-term policy moves (see Revising the SEP: Some benefits of shifting to rolling windows). 2. records.text: M Idea 18 Key Recommendations We're long 15yr basis as valuations on production 15s are near local wides despite 30yr valuations near local tights. The risk the trade is macro uncertainties or supply picking up in 15s. We also like buying DW4.5/FNCL 5 for similar reasons, though the risks to that trade are more about continued demand in 30s and curve hedging strategies. In terms of relative value trades, we like owning 350k and seasoned 4.5s vs TBA at wide OAS vs collateral as a cheap-ish option on a further rates rally. The risk is the negative carry vs the roll and/or selloff. For investors who want mortgage exposure, we prefer owning higher coupons on specs, with preference for 200-300k 6.0s on basis or vs. TBA and 5.0s vs. TBA. We also like Mission 5.5 and 6.0s. Higher coupons have lagged other coupons, but owning call protected versions of these pools reduces some of the convexity exposure and will likely benefit from demand support. The risk is faster speeds and/or macro risk off, along with the challenges in modeling mission pools. We also suggest investors buy secondary floaters for short-duration mortgage exposure, particularly in Ginnies. In Europe, we typically find a smaller real rate decline in response to energy price shocks vs the US. And while higher energy prices would represent a negative terms of trade shock for the Euro area as a whole, the source of recent improvement in growth is due less to lower energy prices than to the ramping German fiscal expansion working its way into the real economy. We think this combination presents hawkish risks for the EUR front-end, although in line with the historical relationship this would likely flatten the curve as negative risk sentiment helps anchor longer term yields. We provide a regular update on the evolution of developed market (DM) rates markets in the recent past. Considering the uncertainty surrounding trade and fiscal policy, we begin by comparing budget balances and current account balances across major DM countries. We then analyse the distribution of outstanding bonds by investor type to assess the proportion held by price-insensitive investors, such as domestic central banks. Moving to market pricing, we examine pricing trends of major central banks, followed by recent market movements in key rates products. With the impact of cyclical factors having been removed, it provides fair value estimates based on long-term structural factors, such as purchasing power parity (i.e. inflation differentials), long-term shifts in the terms of trade and the impact of current account imbalances. FEER provides a long-term anchor point for G10 currency pairs, with misaligned currencies typically taking between two and five years to move into line with their FEERs. The USD’s overvaluation relative to its FEER decreased in 2025, to 20.1% compared to 32% in 2024. This is mainly due to USD weakness as FEERs remain relatively stable. The FEER framework considers the USD overvalued due to the US’s large current account deficit. The EUR continues to appear cheap versus the USD and CHF, while it remains overvalued against the NOK and SEK. records.text: More dire predictions also ignore other margins of adjustment. If AI automation surges, real incomes will rise, relative prices and wages will adjust, and fiscal and monetary policy will respond to help offset near-term job losses. And even if productivity increases much more rapidly than labor demand and job losses are large, political economy dynamics will likely force other margins of adjustment. For example, rapid productivity growth from electrification in the 1910s and 1920s boosted real income. Henry Ford in turn introduced the five-day work week, partially in response to increased worker demand for leisure (with help from increased labor organization and worker bargaining power) and a recognition that an extra day on the weekend would give consumers more time to spend their newly earned money (and increase demand for cars). What are the biggest near-term risks to the labor market from AI? We still see two main near-term downside labor market risks related to AI. In the very near term, the main risk is that the prospect of AI automation leads companies to freeze hiring, thereby slowing the labor market even if jobs are not being displaced. The more significant risk is that a drop in aggregate demand could lead forward-looking companies that are focused on costs to accelerate plans to automate and eliminate positions using generative AI. records.text: Our model points to gradual services disinflation ahead. Using our baseline assumptions for the labour market, goods prices, and wages, we estimate that fading relative price pressures and moderating wage growth will shave 0.5pp off services inflation over the coming year (Exhibit 5, left). This would bring services inflation back to the 2-3% range that has historically aligned with 2% core inflation. At the same time, we expect the labour market to remain robust (with no increase in the unemployment rate) and prevent services inflation from falling below its target-consistent range. The model-implied path is also close to our baseline forecast and the ECB staff projections (Exhibit 5, right). Finally, we use our model to study two alternative scenarios (Exhibit 6). First, we construct a downside scenario in which the unemployment rate rises by 2pp over the next couple for years (for instance, due to AI-induced job losses), leading to a slowdown in wage growth. We estimate that services inflation would fall to 2% in such a case, close to the bottom of its target-consistent range. In 2026, the EU will likely issue EUR 160bn versus EUR 6.5bn in the case of the ESM. The EUR 432bn of unused lending capacity available at the ESM seems to get increasing political attention. On 13 Feb, the EC proposed to transfer the ESM with the EU (see details here): "An area for further reflection is how the architecture of the EU-wide financial safety net could be made more efficient. While proposals have been made in the past on reforming the ESM, the EU regional safety system remains fragmented and only partly anchored in EU institutions. Euro area MS rely on the ESM." At this stage, the proposal by the EC to transfer the ESM to the EU level lacks details how this could be done in practice or for what exactly the unused lending capacity at the ESM should be used for (with defence currently probably the main topic). In our view, transferring the ESM to the EU or reawakening the proposal of the European Monetary Fund (EMF, see details here) is complex from a legal and political perspective. records.text: EQUITIES | CORPORATE MARKETS MONTHLY As new AI technology sends ripples through financial markets, particularly in the technology sector, both winners and losers emerge. Markets 360 is neutral on equities in the near term, with our tactical indicators suggesting reasons to be cautious and use optionality in the current environment. Below we summarise BNP Paribas Equity Research views on the impact of AI on software-as-a-service (SaaS) and semiconductor stocks – for more, see SaaS smash: A playbook in the hunt for a valuation floor (Ben Castillo-Bernaus, Ines Mao, Stefan Slowinski, Andrew DeGasperi, dated 5 February 2026) and Absolutely fabulous 2026 – Tracking EUV capacity (Jakob Bluestone CFA, and Kohulan Paramaguru CFA, dated 2 February 2026). SaaS: BNP Paribas Equity Research finds that IT-services companies in Europe are priced for negative growth due to the AI threat, but vertical-software stocks aren’t pricing in long-term growth disruption, which presents a downside risk. Nevertheless, the sector overall trades at 15x FCF (median), a 35% discount to spot 10y yield, according to the analysts. Concerns of long-term disruption from AI innovation have been driving severe selling in many software and IT-services stocks this year, even after a de-rating of about 20% in H2 2025. Given the valuation compression seen, the analysts’ discussions with investors have shifted away from fundamentals and towards considerations for potential valuation support levels. records.text: 27 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 91 Tariffs post IEEPA Today’s CoTD shows updated projections for the average US import tariff rate and implied custom duty revenue following last Friday’s Supreme Court ruling on IEEPA tariffs. We estimate that without the latter and no replacement, the average tariff rate would have fallen by ~6.5pp ( Figure 166); assuming an across-the-board section 122 tariff rate of 15% along with unchanged exemptions would imply a decline of ~2pp5 . Across the main trading partners, China sees the largest relief. In terms of fiscal revenues, as argued last week, actual duties have been running at a monthly run rate at ~USD28bn, or 336bn annualised (1.1% of GDP), i.e. below the most recent CBO projections. Tariff revenue could be expected to fall to ~0.45% of GDP without IEEPA, and to ~0.85% with a 15% section 122 replacement. With no clarity about potential refunds and an immediate broad replacement tariff implementation, we are not expecting a significant disinflationary impact from last week’s decision. Higher tariffs have pushed up consumer goods prices and have put upward pressure on production costs which implies further risks of indirect effects for CPI going forward. Against this backdrop, the risk is that inflation will stay at above-target levels this year despite slowing rental inflation and our CPI forecasts remain above front-end market valuations. There is some evidence of the latter: in Q4, BAC reduced its Treasury holdings by $17bn and reserve balances by $21bn despite a modestly higher deposit base. System-wide, bank deposits increased by $327bn in the last quarter, while securities holdings fell by $29bn, including a $12bn drop in Treasury holdings. Historically, deposits and securities tend to move in the same direction. The divergence may then suggest broader LCR optimization by banks to reduce regulatory drag. That said, we expect the effects on major ratios (unemployment rate, participation rate, emp loyment-to-population ratio) to be minimal , albeit with an elevated surprise potential. In 2022–24, the BLS serially underestimated the size of the population amid high immigration flows. This resulted in a large upward adjustment in the population controls in January 2025 of nearly three million. However, updated data from the Census Bureau, which feeds into the BLS estimates, suggest that the BLS has been overestimating population growth since late -2024. This should mean a downward adjustment in this year’s iteration (Figure 7). We estimate the population aged 16-and-over will be revised down by about 590k in the refreshed January data, that the labor force will be revised down by about 370k, with a similar cut to the level of household survey employment. While the official BLS data will still show the labor force rising by three million in 2025 (the data is not revised), the true growth was likely much lower. Using an experimental BLS series that smooths for past population controls and immigration, and incorporating the latest vintage of Census Bureau data, we estimate the labor force grew by only 900k in 2025 and expect overall labor force growth of well less than 500k in 2026. records.text: Global Multi-Asset Strategy 01 March 2026 Citi Research 11 EM credit impact GCC credit is likely to come under pressure following the weekend’s developments. Previous periods of Middle East tension did not significantly affect Gulf assets, as markets assumed conflicts would remain contained. The current situation is different. Missiles and drones were launched directly at GCC territory for the first time in many years. For instance, DP World suspended its operations in Jebel Ali port, which will impact the company (Bloomberg, 01-Mar-26), while some hotel infrastructure as well as airports were also damaged in the attacks (Haaretz, 01-Mar-26). These events represent a material shock to a region long viewed as stable and somewhat insulated from global volatility. GCC credit had benefited from strong sovereign balance sheets, high IG ratings, and steady demand from Asia. That demand was supported by tighter supply conditions in Asian credit markets. The latest attacks now challenge the region’s safe-haven status, something that previous escalations never tested. Within the GCC, UAE credit may come under greater strain. Headlines have focused heavily on the attacks there, amplifying investor concerns. While a unilateral withdrawal from the USMCA would have significant repercussions for the United States economy; the impact on Canada and Mexico would be even more severe. Currently, 72% of Canada’s exports are directed to the United States, with Canada -US trade accounting for one third of Canada’s overall economy. The proportion of goods qualifying for USMCA exemption has increased from 58% in 2021 to over 70% in 2025 (Figure 4). Should the United States depart from the USMCA without an immediate successor agreement, Canada -US trade would revert to WTO most favoured nation (MFN) terms, resulting in the loss of zero -tariff access, rules -based dispute mechanisms, protections for services, digital trade, and procurement. records.text: 27 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 87 Summary of Jan/Feb EGB Supply In yesterday’s piece Who bought EGBs in Jan/Feb? we analysed the composition of demand for EGBs through the allocations of syndications that took place in the first two months of the year. In today’s FICOTD, with all supply filled, we look at the supply statistics for the usually heaviest supply months of the year. January was the heaviest EGB supply month on record (EUR 195bn), and although February (EUR 140bn) saw a drop in volumes, it once again came with a higher WAM (weighted average maturity) of issuance, i.e. at 12.4 years vs 10.6 years in January. Once compared vs the official issuance plans for the entire year, we estimate a 23.5% completion rate in Jan & Feb, exactly the same as last year. The WAM of Jan & Feb EGB supply is estimated at 11.4 years, slightly higher than the 11.1 years seen last year, hence not confirming the anticipated drop in WAM for now. However, given the impact of syndications (in their majority long-dated) in Jan & Feb issuance, the WAM should start dropping from March onwards as has been the case historically. As a reminder, the WAM of EGB supply in 2025 ended up at around 10 years, lower than where it was at the end of February. In terms of country comparison, we have the usual pattern where smaller issuers have already filled a larger chunk of their planned annual issuance because their syndications form a larger share of total bond supply. While 30yr MBS spreads are near the tights of the past four years, 15-year spreads look more attractive to us. Historically, 30yr current coupon OAS has traded wider than 15yr given greater negative convexity risk. However, that relationship flipped a few months ago and 15yr CC OAS is now trading significantly wider instead. While expectation for GSE buying in 30s may explain some of the move, we note that other 15yr relationships (such as 15yr-30yr yield difference vs. curve, or 15yr issuance % vs. curve) have also decoupled lately. The difference between 15y and (+50bp) 30y spreads are near the wides across the coupon stack for both OAS and ZV, implying that discrepancy isn't necessarily driven by vol either. When we went to SFIG Vegas this week, one of the main themes from the conference from agency MBS investors was a collective grumbling that spreads, at near the tights of the last four years, are rather difficult to get excited about here. While that may be true on the 30-year side, in this report we highlight that the same is not true for 15s. records.text: Global Synthesis Trading fear Amid scant fresh data, markets continued to trade erratically on AI worries, including some unrealistic scenarios. Although disruption will likely be part of the AI-adoption path, this may take longer than markets expect. US payrolls will offer more insight, while Iran is the imminent risk. The AI fear factor 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself' , Franklin D Roosevelt famously told his audience in his 1933 inauguration speech. At the time, the US was in the depths of the Great Depression, with over 25% unemployment and failing banks. FDR wanted to stress that the real danger was not these material problems themselves, but the powerful emotion of fear, which could paralyse people, preventing them from taking necessary action, or, on the opposite, trigger irrational, excessive reactions. In recent weeks, at a time when the US macro outlook is far from what FDR faced in 1933, with robust growth, low unemployment and stable banks, fear has become a driver in financial markets nevertheless. This time, the fear is about the potential consequences of AI, a technology that in principle should bring immense increases in productivity. The United States currently conducts more trade with Mexico and Canada collectively than with China (Figure 3). According to the IMF, the USMCA has contributed to a roughly 2% increase in US output over time. Trade associated with the USMCA supports millions of jobs across key sectors including agriculture, automotive, machinery, logistics, and services. Specifically, agricultu ral trade alone accounts for approximately 50 0K jobs. The automotive industry would be particularly affected, as parts frequently cross borders multiple times, and the removal of rules of origin would diminish protections for domestic firms. Furthermore, eliminating robust digital trade, IP, and data - flow safeguards could impede major technology and financial services companies. Taken together , abandoning the USMCA would likely result in reduced potential economic growth, increased production costs for US manufacturers, and greater regional disparities, especially impacting states in the Midwest, the great plains, and along the border. records.text: China Outlook More easing likely around the annual NPC We expect the NPC to lower the GDP growth target to 4.5-5.0% for 2026, and keep the budget deficit broadly flat at around 4% of GDP . We think the more important event that will shape the China tariff outlook and the China-US relationship is the highly anticipated Trump-Xi meeting. Watch for more monetary easing around the NPC meeting China’s annual “Two Sessions” will begin next week, with the NPC session opening on 5 March. Around 2,900 delegates from across the country will gather to discuss macroeconomic policies and socio-economic priorities. Premier Li Qiang will deliver the annual Government Work Report (GWR) on the first day of the NPC session, reviewing the past year’s performance and setting out key policy tasks and economic targets for this year, including GDP growth, fiscal spending, employment, and inflation, to list a few. The authorities are also expected to release the 15th Five-Year Plan (FYP), outlining policy objectives for 2026–2030 (China: The Fourth Plenum: forging ahead, 23 October 2025) We expect the GDP growth target for 2026 to be lowered to 4.5–5% from last year target of around 5%, given that 21 out of 31 provincial-level governments reduced their 2026 growth targets by 0-50bp from 2025 levels in their local “Two Sessions” held in January to early February. Mind the gap: Tariff collections peaked at roughly USD25bn (about USD300bn annualised) in May 2025, then declined to a monthly run-rate near USD20bn (about USD260bn annualised) over December–January. Throughout the past year, actual tariff revenues have fallen short of the levels projected based on our estimate of the effective tariff rate. In other words, the tariff rate implied by collections (‘collected/effective’ tariff rate) has been consistently lower than the rate stipulated by law (‘statutory’ tariff rate). The primary factor behind the discrepancy – and the basis for our Q4 2025 downward revision of the statutory tariff rate – is the volume of USMCA-compliant imports from Mexico and Canada. In a dynamic AI-enabled economy, we find it quite plausible that a moderate step up in the pace of job creation could boost gross job gains enough to absorb most AI-related job losses and leave employment levels roughly unchanged. We also take some comfort in the fact that there are several channels through which AI might create new jobs, including expanding markets via lower costs and improved efficiency, creating new roles in AI-adjacent positions, facilitating increased occupational specialization, and boosting demand for discretionary service workers via higher real income. Furthermore, we note potential for technological replacement does not always lead to job loss. For instance, employment of fitness instructors (who were replaceable in the 1980s by fitness tapes and even more so today with the proliferation of fitness apps) and real estate agents (whose role as an intermediary has largely been replaced by online platforms) has outperformed overall employment both recently and over the last 25 years. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 39 Weekly Summary for Overseas Investors Market Recap We received a lot of news this week across a number of sources; however, we think the most important piece of information out this week may have come from the exciting world of accounting standards. FASB discussed allowing banks to hedge interest rate risk of HTM securities, which further aligns with banks coming back amid less regulation. What this change would do is allow banks to buy bonds into HTM and hedge interest rate exposure without having to apply any spread changes to earnings or concern about LCR impact. That could potentially result in more bank demand for securities, less reserves needed, and wider swap spreads as bank buying of UST vs swaps increases as well. The American Bankers Association believes that the draft could be issued in the second quarter with final standard release by the end of this year, if not earlier. China's NPC: Lower growth, unchanged fiscal and easier monetary In China, the focus next week will be on the National People's Congress starting on 5 March, at which the premier will lay out key economic targets, such as GDP growth and fiscal spending. We expect the GDP growth target for 2026 to be lowered to 4.5–5.0% from last year's target of around 5%, given the reductions in targets by many provincial governments. If confirmed, this would mark the first downward adjustment to the annual GDP growth target in four years. In our view, such a recalibration would signal a pragmatic approach in light of the structural challenges domestically and external headwinds facing the economy, while the expected target range would provide policymakers with greater flexibility to respond to changing circumstances. On policy, we expect the budget deficit to remain broadly flat at around 4% of GDP . The December CEWC statement highlighted the need to maintain a 'necessary' fiscal deficit and spending, marking a shift from last year's message, which pledged to raise the fiscal deficit ratio and issue more ultra-long special treasury bonds to fund higher spending. We also continue to expect some monetary policy easing, including a 10bp cut in the policy rate and a 50bp RRR cut in Q1. In the past, the PBoC has delivered such moves ahead of the NPC. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W Central bank gold buying seen rising again in 2026: Central banks purchased 397.1 tonnes (12.8 moz) of gold last year, up 7% on 2024 and highest rate of buying in three years. Volumes remained well short of the 2015 high of 913.4 tonnes (29.4 moz) which had been largely driven by the PBoC buying 708.2 tonnes (22.8 moz), but we expect volumes to grow again this year to well in excess of 400 tonnes. We see this gold accumulation trend as supportive for positive price sentiment. Poland’s central bank (NBP) was the most significant official sector gold purchaser in 2025, accumulating 102 tonnes (3.3 moz), up 14% y/y. On 20 January this year, the NBP approved plans to buy a further 150 tonnes (4.8 moz), which would take its holdings to 700 tonnes (22.5 moz). However, the approval did not specify a timescale for this additional accumulation. China’s PBoC reportedly bought 26.7 tonnes (860 koz) of gold last year, with volumes dropping sharply through Q4 as gold prices surged – October to December monthly volumes averaged only 0.9 tonnes (30 koz). In January, however, volumes jumped to 1.2 tonnes (40 koz). Although one month is not a trend, we do expect further moves to de-dollarise by the PBoC through 2026, suggesting to us that gold purchasing volumes may well be higher in 2026 than in 2025. The oil price is likely to spike based on events to date, and we would expect Brent in the low to mid-80s as the initial reaction to the weekend events (it reached $79 in June 2025 at the peak of geopolitical risks). Iranian exports will be limited at the very least for the duration of the conflict, and possibly longer depending on the actions of Iran’s leadership (with the potential for Venezuela-style export restrictions). Whether the price spike is sustained and how high it goes, depends on the actual and expected impact on global oil supply. The longer-term fundamental impact will depend on several factors, including what the new Iranian leader (once chosen following the death of Ayatollah Khamenei) and the remaining Iranian regime leadership choose to do in the coming days. Namely, the key questions are whether they escalate or not, whether Iran targets regional oil assets, or whether they attempt to reach a settlement. It is difficult to see a credible path to a negotiated outcome in the near term, making the outlook highly uncertain. Headlines around potential Strait of Hormuz closure are unlikely to be sustained given the military presence in the region as well as Iran’s reliance on oil exports. records.text: Labour market holds the key What about the labour market, where adoption should be reflected in jobs losses, assuming that AI will not only be complementary, but in large parts also lead to full automation to substitute human workers? Signs of AI-related reallocation, but not broader unemployment We last did a comprehensive study of this last May using the data between 2017 and 2024 (recall that ChatGPT was publicly released in November 2022, so this sample covers the early days of generative AI). At the time, we did not find robust evidence that AI is reducing employment in the aggregate. In fact, we saw some signs of the opposite, ie, firms, industries or occupations more exposed to AI experiencing faster employment growth. For more recent evidence, we can look at job postings and payrolls in a sector particularly at risk of substitution: software development. Here, the evidence is mixed. Both payrolls and job postings have declined in recent years. However, the decline began before even ChatGPT was released (and, realistically, it would take some time before AI would be developed and adopted to the extent that most corporates would be prepared to alter their hiring plans in response to it). Also, the recent declines come after a large ramp-up during the pandemic and they have been slower and smaller than after the dot-com bust (computer systems payrolls are currently c.100k below the peak; in the early 2000s, the peak-to-trough decline was 250k). Tariffs on Japanese products had previously been set in principle at 15%, including for automobiles, under the US-Japan agreement that included USD550bn of investment in the US. As a result, even if the uniform tariff is raised from 10% to 15%, Japan’s average effective tariff rate would likely to remain broadly unchanged. According to estimates by Global Trade Alert (GTA), Japan’s effective tariff rate was 14.90% before the Supreme Court ruling and would be 13.54% under a uniform 10% tariff or 15.35% if the rate were increased to 15%. That said, whereas previously the rule was that tariffs were capped at 15% inclusive of existing rates, or that existing rates applied if they were 15% or higher, under the new uniform tariff, the 10% (or 15%) is added on top of existing rates depending on the product. This means that tariff rates could end up somewhat higher than before. For this reason, on the 23rd Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Akazawa requested US Commerce Secretary Lutnick to ensure that Japan’s tariff burden does not increase. Meanwhile, the government has indicated that it will continue to implement investment in the US, which had been a quid pro quo for tariff reductions. To measure geopolitical risk, we use the GPR index developed by Fed Board staff (Caldara and Iacoviello), which is based on the number of articles in a set of top newspapers that are related to adverse geopolitical threats and actions (e.g., wars, military buildups, terrorism). As a baseline, we use the headline monthly index (available back to 1985), though as discussed below also explore the robustness of our findings using the daily GPR index. The left chart plots geopolitical shocks (measured as the month-on-month index change) on the x-axis and the corresponding change in 10y UST on the y-axis; the largest shocks over the last thirty years are separately labelled. Most striking is that these have almost all been associated with higher yields, contrary to a view that geopolitical risk is inherently bullish for duration through safe-haven flows. Of course, as the labels on the big shocks make clear, most have been associated with energy supply disruptions and so would be expected to boost yields through higher oil prices. records.text: 27 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 35 One potential way that regulators could tweak the LCR is to allow for non-HQLA assets prepositioned at the discount window and available to borrow through primary credit loans to count toward the total HQLA figure in the numerator. In the current rules, banks receive no credit for prepositioned collateral despite the potential credit they may draw down from the discount window in a stress event. Bowman has previously discussed validating the use of the discount window in the regulatory framework to help destigmatize the facility. With approximately $1.8tn in lendable value of loan collateral prepositioned at the discount window, and LCR-subject domestic banks (>$250bn assets) accounting for roughly 2/3 of total domestic bank assets, this change could generate a benefit of ~$1.2tn in additional HQLA. Other potential adjustments that have been floated are to dynamically adjust the LCR downward in stress events or to allow discount window borrowing to reduce net cash outflows in the denominator of the LCR. However, unlike ILSTs that directly impact a bank’s decision to hold reserves vs repo or Treasuries through their overnight testing horizon, the LCR does not affect that as reserves, repo, and Treasuries are all treated the same in the calculation. To control for this and isolate the impact of geopolitics through other channels, we run an OLS regression of the m/m change in 10y UST over the past thirty years on four variables: the change in spot oil prices, economic data surprises, geopolitical shocks, and economic policy uncertainty shocks (measured using Baker Bloom Davis). The results are shown in the right chart, which plots the estimated impact on 10y UST (in bps) of a +1-standard deviation move in each variable and the associated 90-percent confidence intervals. The results indicate that positive oil price moves and data surprises significantly lift yields, higher policy uncertainty lowers them, and geopolitical shocks have no direct impact. These findings are robust to running the analysis on daily instead of monthly data, entering the geopolitical and policy uncertainty indexes in levels rather than changes, and including the lagged change in the 10y UST as a regressor to control for any yield-momentum effects. Together, this suggests that, as far as UST yields are concerned, the main mechanism / variable to track on current Iran developments is the price of oil. More negative labor market predictions do not fully account for the dynamic n nature of the labor market, in our opinion. The US economy creates more than 30mn gross new jobs per year, and technological change is the main driver of long-run employment growth. We expect that these dynamics will repeat and AI will create new jobs while it destroys others. We therefore do not anticipate a job apocalypse. We will be monitoring AI adoption trends, the hiring drag on jobs already n affected by AI, and the correlation between AI adoption and labor market slack indicators to gauge AI progress and risks. Among specific credits, BHRAIN is especially fragile to any substantial escalation, given its pre-existing fiscal issues, its dependence on the Straits of Hormuz, and a prolonged regional conflict potentially reducing or delaying an already-uncertain GCC bailout necessary to stabilize debt dynamics. QATAR and KUWAIT are similarly exposed to closures in the Straits of Hormuz, given their lack of access to the Red Sea. Large oil importers – Egypt, Türkiye – are likely to face inflationary pressures from higher oil prices and cross-asset pressures from their especially well-positioned local currency assets. records.text: Risks to Oil Prices Supply at Risk Q2. Is oil infrastructure in Iran and the Middle East damaged? To our knowledge, there is no confirmed damage to oil production or to oil export infrastructure in the region.1 Q3. How much oil supply from Iran and from the Middle East via the Strait of Hormuz is at risk? Iran produced around 3.5mb/d of crude oil and about 0.8mb/d of condensate in 2025, together worth 4% of global oil supply. Iran’s 2025 exports averaged 1.7mb/d for crude and condensates, 0.6mb/d for refined products, and 0.4mb/d for Natural Gas Liquids (NGLs).2 The Strait is crucial for nearly 20mb/d or 1/5 of global oil production (Exhibit 1). Exports in 2025 through the Strait averaged 13.4mb/d for crude, 0.2mb/d for condensates, 3.5mb/d for refined products, and 1.4mb/d for NGLs and other liquids. Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the UAE together exported 13.1mb/d of oil via the Strait of Hormuz last year, with China as the main destination (Exhibit 12). While estimates vary across agencies, the IEA has estimated that 4.2mb/d of the oil flows through the Strait can be redirected using existing spare pipeline capacities, implying around 16mb/d of oil flows at risk from a hypothetical full closure of the Strait.3 1 That said, Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency reported on Saturday an explosion at the Kharg Island oil export terminal, which handles over 90% of Iran crude exports. From the demand side, the labor market’s weakness (Figure 3) suggests muted private consumption (Figure 4) this year. In addition, the BCRA’s latest quarterly credit survey showed weaker credit demand over the last two quarters (especially for corporates), which is an ominous sign for credit dynamics (Figure 5). Moreover, the impact of the rise in nonperforming loans (which peaked for individuals at 9%) could complicate the supply of credit too. Regarding the economy’s remonetization, while the real exchange rate is not as low as it was before the FX market’s unification, it is probably at a level that coexists with depreciation expectations. Our base case is that the jobless rate averages around 4.3% this year, with a slight tilt lower to 4.2% in 2027. We think that keeps the Fed on the sidelines, with little need to lean against cyclical weakness with rate cuts. This sort of uneasy balance in the job market – low job gains, but also low unemployment – is uncomfortable, but sustainable. We remain upbeat on the economy’s prospects in 2026 (see US: K-shaped capex nets to stronger near-term growth, dated 24 February). Risks to the unemployment rate are bidirectional. Stimulative fiscal policy, stimulative monetary policy and stimulative financial conditions are now in place, and trade-policy uncertainty, which likely held back hiring in 2025, is now easing. These could set the stage for a cyclical pickup in 2026. Downside risk to the labor market, in our view, probably comes from further shedding of pandemic-era ‘labor hoards’ or the scaling of AI in the business sector (outside of the technology industry) earlier than we currently expect.

records.text: 27 February 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG be delayed. The Commission is looking for ways to speed up reform. Recently it was announced there could be areas where coalitions of at least 9 countries move forward with policy changes. Today's trade deal announcement ties with those efforts to accelerate the pace of change. ECB speakers On Wednesday Vujcic had his hearing in front of the ECON committee of the EU Parliament as part of the nomination process for ECB Vice President. His prepared remarks and responses to MEP questions did not give too much away as he stuck close to the public views of the ECB. The ECB also released their statement that they have no objections to his candidacy (one of the required steps in the nomination process). We lean to the view that tariff refunds are not mandated and President Trump will use section- based tariffs to restore the effective tariff rate. Regardless, the knee-jerk market reaction is likely to be negative for rates, given tariff revenue is a key reason why deficits improved in 2025 and was expected to offset the effects of the One Big Beautiful Bill. Any possibility of tariff refunds or doubts around fully restoring the effective tariff rate could drive markets to question US debt sustainability. President Trump also recently floated the prospect of allocating an extra USD500bn for the defense budget, which could lift 10y and 30y UST term premiums. records.text: United Kingdom Outlook Gorton goes Green A win for the Green Party in this week's by-election raises the risk of political uncertainty over the coming months. Meanwhile, the Q2 Ofgem cap led us to revise up our inflation forecast at the margin and surveys pointed to welcome progress on inflation expectations in February. • The Green party won the Gorton and Denton by-election, with Labour pushed into third place, raising the risk of further speculation about a leadership challenge in coming weeks. Next week, the chancellor will deliver the Spring statement. We do not expect any policy changes and only minor changes in forecasts from the OBR. • The Q2 Ofgem price cap for this year was announced, implying a 6.6% contraction in energy bills, a smaller deflation than our forecast. Our updated inflation forecast leaves the 2026 annual average unchanged at 2.2%, but 2027 was revised upwards (+0.1pp to 2.0%). Inflation expectations measured by YouGov/Citi and also GfK eased in February. • The MPC speakers this week did not change our outlook for the March meeting, where we still expect a cut. The key data releases between now and the meeting are the DMP survey (5 March), January GDP data (13 March), and the February employment data, due to be released publicly on the morning of the meeting (19 March). records.text: out diffusion: Where are we on the sigmoid function? Why are markets so receptive to a fictional doomsday scenario? Because they sense that: a) parts of the financial sector look quite vulnerable, with highly priced AI stocks, intransparent private equity constructs, etc, and that b) AI has the potential to be very disruptive. Indeed, sharp increases in unemployment and rapid profit losses in disrupted sectors are possible, even if the notion of a 'ghost GDP' is wrong. The path towards an AI-transformed, higher-productivity, higher growth world is likely paved with the need for massive resource reallocation and potential crises. Keynes and the Great Depression taught us that a simplistic version of Say's law, assuming 'supply always creates its own demand' , may not hold. If AI-related disruption is a justified underlying worry, then the question is how soon it could occur. If the history of technological innovation and its adoption is any guide, the disruption may take some time. The adoption of new technologies throughout the whole economy typically occurs long after the original innovation or invention. The diffusion typically follows a sigmoid function, the graph of which has a characteristic S-shape. Hence, it starts slow, then takes off and then slows again. For example, annual mobile phone sales since 1997 conform to such a logistic curve with the inflection point in 2008. 1 27 February 2026 4 Barclays | Global Economics Weekly: Trading fear

envision a significant hit to entry-level positions over the next few years. That said, most of the doomsday predictions ignore that the economy is very dynamic. Most importantly, we have argued AI will create many new jobs at the same time that it destroys others. Exhibit 11 summarizes research from David Autor and coauthors that shows how important this force has been both over the long run. Using data from the Census Bureau’s Alphabetical Indexes of Industries and Occupations, they find that 60% of workers today are employed in occupations that did not exist in 1940. This means that over 85% of the job gains over the last 85 years have been driven by the creative destruction process. A natural concern is that, even if new jobs are created, the 1-4mn/year peak annual job losses shown in Exhibit 9 could overwhelm the labor market, which adds a few million net jobs per year at most. There is historical precedent that justifies these worries to some degree. Economists Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo showed that as companies adopted information and communication technologies in the 1990s and early 2000s the pace of job creation struggled to keep up with the pace of job destruction, giving rise to a period of jobless growth. Comparing AI displacement projections to net job growth understates the dynamism of the labor market, however. records.text: 27 February 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 86 Deutsche Bank AG A curious shift in bank deposits in Q4 Something curious took place in bank deposits in Q4, according to FDIC data released this week. Last quarter saw a significant compositional shift, with non- transaction savings deposits declining by $744bn, while transaction account deposits increasing by $1,062bn. Deposit mix matters because it feeds directly into the calculation of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), which in turn influences demand for Treasuries and central bank reserves. From an LCR standpoint, transaction deposits can improve a bank’s LCR as they tend to be operational in nature and carry lower 30-day outflow assumptions. That said, actual outflow rates are internally modelled and depend more on depositor characteristics than the account label itself. (For a related discussion of LCR and reserve demand, see: “ Fixed Income Blog: Reserve demand and deregulations”.) Call Report data show that one institution drove essentially the entire shift: Bank of America (BAC). This effectively rules out an industry-wide regulatory change or migration of deposits. The magnitude of the shift also makes it unlikely that one bank experienced deposit flows of that size within one single quarter. There also wasn't any meaningful discussion of deposit mix changes or LCR implications on BAC’s Q4 earnings call. This leaves the most plausible explanation as a classification mapping change in BAC’s Call Report, either as

In Europe, we typically find a smaller real rate decline in response to energy price shocks vs the US. And while higher energy prices would represent a negative terms of trade shock for the Euro area as a whole, the source of recent improvement in growth is due less to lower energy prices than to the ramping German fiscal expansion working its way into the real economy. We think this combination presents hawkish risks for the EUR front-end, although in line with the historical relationship this would likely flatten the curve as negative risk sentiment helps anchor longer term yields.
